theory.intro: When you know two sides and a non-included angle (an **SSA** triangle), the sine rule can give **two** triangles. Because $\sin\theta=\sin(180^{\circ}-\theta)$, both the acute answer $\theta$ and its obtuse partner $180^{\circ}-\theta$ may fit. Find both, then test each against the $180^{\circ}$ angle sum.
facts: The sine rule $\dfrac{\sin B}{b}=\dfrac{\sin A}{a}$ gives $\sin B$, which may have an acute **and** an obtuse solution.
Find the acute angle $\theta=\sin^{-1}(\ldots)$, then its obtuse partner $\theta'=180^{\circ}-\theta$.
The obtuse solution $\theta'$ is valid only if $\theta'+(\text{given angle})<180^{\circ}$; otherwise reject it.
If the given angle is already obtuse, there is at most **one** solution, since a triangle can have at most one obtuse angle.
steps: Use the sine rule to find the acute angle $\theta$, keeping the calculator value
Add each possible angle to the given angle and reject any whose sum reaches $180^{\circ}$
State all valid values of the angle, rounding only at the end

workedExamples.question_text:
Two triangles have sides $6$ cm and $5$ cm. The angle opposite the $5$ cm side is $30^{\circ}$.
Find both possible values of the angle $\theta$ opposite the $6$ cm side, correct to the nearest degree.
workedExamples.solution_text:
$\dfrac{\sin\theta}{6}=\dfrac{\sin30^{\circ}}{5}$
$\sin\theta=\dfrac{6\sin30^{\circ}}{5}=0.6$
$\theta=\sin^{-1}(0.6)\approx36.8699^{\circ}$
$\theta'=180^{\circ}-\theta\approx143.1301^{\circ}$
$143.1301^{\circ}+30^{\circ}<180^{\circ}$, so both angles are valid.
$\theta\approx37^{\circ}$ or $143^{\circ}$.

workedExamples.question_text:
A triangle has sides $4$ cm and $10$ cm. The angle opposite the $10$ cm side is $30^{\circ}$.
Find the angle $\theta$ opposite the $4$ cm side, correct to the nearest degree.
workedExamples.solution_text:
$\dfrac{\sin\theta}{4}=\dfrac{\sin30^{\circ}}{10}$
$\sin\theta=\dfrac{4\sin30^{\circ}}{10}=0.2$
$\theta=\sin^{-1}(0.2)\approx11.5370^{\circ}$
$\theta'=180^{\circ}-\theta\approx168.4630^{\circ}$
$168.4630^{\circ}+30^{\circ}>180^{\circ}$, so the obtuse partner is rejected.
$\theta\approx12^{\circ}$ only.

workedExamples.question_text:
A triangle has sides $5$ cm and $10$ cm. The angle opposite the $10$ cm side is $120^{\circ}$.
Find the angle $\theta$ opposite the $5$ cm side, correct to the nearest degree.
workedExamples.solution_text:
$\dfrac{\sin\theta}{5}=\dfrac{\sin120^{\circ}}{10}$
$\sin\theta=\dfrac{5\sin120^{\circ}}{10}$
$\theta=\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{5\sin120^{\circ}}{10}\right)\approx25.6589^{\circ}$
$\theta'=180^{\circ}-\theta\approx154.3411^{\circ}$
$154.3411^{\circ}+120^{\circ}>180^{\circ}$, so the obtuse partner is rejected.
$25.6589^{\circ}+120^{\circ}<180^{\circ}$, so the acute angle is valid.
$\theta\approx26^{\circ}$ only.

workedExamples.question_text:
A triangle is claimed to have sides $9$ cm and $4$ cm. The angle opposite the $4$ cm side is $30^{\circ}$.
Try to find the angle $\theta$ opposite the $9$ cm side and explain why the triangle is impossible.
workedExamples.solution_text:
$\dfrac{\sin\theta}{9}=\dfrac{\sin30^{\circ}}{4}$
$\sin\theta=\dfrac{9\sin30^{\circ}}{4}=1.125$
Since $\sin\theta$ cannot exceed $1$, no such triangle exists.

workedExamples.question_text:
In triangle $PQR$, $p=7$ cm, $q=10$ cm and $\angle P=30^{\circ}$.
Find both possible sizes of $\angle Q$, correct to the nearest degree, and the corresponding lengths of side $r$, correct to $1$ decimal place.
workedExamples.solution_text:
$\dfrac{\sin Q}{10}=\dfrac{\sin30^{\circ}}{7}$
$\sin Q=\dfrac{10\sin30^{\circ}}{7}=\dfrac57$
$Q_1=\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac57\right)\approx45.5847^{\circ}$
$Q_2=180^{\circ}-Q_1\approx134.4153^{\circ}$
$134.4153^{\circ}+30^{\circ}<180^{\circ}$, so both angles are valid.
Keep the calculator values for the side calculations.
$R_1=180^{\circ}-30^{\circ}-Q_1\approx104.4153^{\circ}$
$r_1=\dfrac{7\sin R_1}{\sin30^{\circ}}\approx13.5592$ cm
$R_2=180^{\circ}-30^{\circ}-Q_2\approx15.5847^{\circ}$
$r_2=\dfrac{7\sin R_2}{\sin30^{\circ}}\approx3.7613$ cm
The possibilities are $Q\approx46^{\circ}$ with $r\approx13.6$ cm, or $Q\approx134^{\circ}$ with $r\approx3.8$ cm.

mastery.question_text:
In triangle $PQR$, $p=7$ is opposite $\angle P=45^{\circ}$ and $q=9$ is opposite $\angle Q$.
Find both possible sizes of $\angle Q$, correct to the nearest degree, and the corresponding length of side $r$, correct to $1$ decimal place.
mastery.solution_text:
$\dfrac{\sin Q}{9}=\dfrac{\sin45^{\circ}}{7}$
$\sin Q=\dfrac{9\sin45^{\circ}}{7}$
$Q_1=\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{9\sin45^{\circ}}{7}\right)\approx65.39^{\circ}$
$Q_2=180^{\circ}-Q_1\approx114.61^{\circ}$
$114.61^{\circ}+45^{\circ}<180^{\circ}$, so both are valid.
Keep the calculator values for the side calculations.
$R_1=180^{\circ}-45^{\circ}-Q_1\approx69.61^{\circ}$
$r_1=\dfrac{7\sin R_1}{\sin45^{\circ}}\approx9.2794$
$R_2=180^{\circ}-45^{\circ}-Q_2\approx20.39^{\circ}$
$r_2=\dfrac{7\sin R_2}{\sin45^{\circ}}\approx3.4485$
The possibilities are $Q\approx65^{\circ}$ with $r\approx9.3$, or $Q\approx115^{\circ}$ with $r\approx3.4$.

mastery.question_text:
In triangle $ABC$, $a=13$ is opposite $\angle A=54^{\circ}$ and $b=7$ is opposite $\angle B$.
Find $\angle B$, correct to the nearest degree, and all possible lengths of side $c$, correct to $1$ decimal place.
mastery.solution_text:
$\dfrac{\sin B}{7}=\dfrac{\sin54^{\circ}}{13}$
$\sin B=\dfrac{7\sin54^{\circ}}{13}$
$B=\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{7\sin54^{\circ}}{13}\right)\approx25.83^{\circ}$
$B'=180^{\circ}-B\approx154.17^{\circ}$
$154.17^{\circ}+54^{\circ}>180^{\circ}$, so the obtuse partner is rejected.
Keep the calculator value of $B$ for the side calculation.
$C=180^{\circ}-54^{\circ}-B\approx100.17^{\circ}$
$c=\dfrac{13\sin C}{\sin54^{\circ}}\approx15.8162$
There is one triangle, with $B\approx26^{\circ}$ and $c\approx15.8$.

mastery.question_text:
In triangle $ABC$, $a=6$ cm is opposite $\angle A=30^{\circ}$ and $b=10$ cm is opposite $\angle B$.
Find all possible sizes of $\angle B$, correct to the nearest degree.
mastery.solution_text:
$\dfrac{\sin B}{10}=\dfrac{\sin30^{\circ}}{6}$
$\sin B=\dfrac{10\sin30^{\circ}}{6}=\dfrac56$
$B=\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac56\right)\approx56.44^{\circ}$
$B'=180^{\circ}-B\approx123.56^{\circ}$
$123.56^{\circ}+30^{\circ}<180^{\circ}$, so both are valid.
$\angle B\approx56^{\circ}$ or $124^{\circ}$.
